introduction: On this Sunday, Naaman the Syrian is healed of leprosy and returns to give thanks to the God of Israel. In the Gospel, Jesus heals ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank him. Paul, in chains, writes, Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead; the word of God is not chained. Let us learn to give thanks.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord has done marvelous things for us. With grateful hearts, let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that her whole life may be a song of thanksgiving, above all in the Eucharist. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the sick, especially those with illnesses that isolate them from others: that they may find healing and companionship. Let us pray to the Lord.
For foreigners and outsiders: that they may be welcomed, as Jesus welcomed the grateful Samaritan. Let us pray to the Lord.
For prisoners, and for all who suffer for the Gospel: that they may know that God's word is not chained. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may never forget to thank God for his gifts. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, every good gift comes from you. Give us grateful hearts, so that we may return to give you thanks for all you have done for us. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Where are the nine?
reflection.body:
Naaman is a Syrian army commander with leprosy. The prophet Elisha tells him to wash seven times in the Jordan, and after some resistance, he does, and "his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child." Then Naaman goes back to the prophet and says, "See now, I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel." His healing leads him to faith and to thanksgiving.

In the Gospel, ten lepers keep their distance from Jesus, as the law required, and call out: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!" He tells them to go and show themselves to the priests, and "As they went, they were cleansed." They trusted his word before they saw the healing.

But only one comes back. "One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan." Jesus asks, "Weren't the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?" And he says to the Samaritan, "Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you." All ten were healed, but the one who returned received something more: a relationship with Jesus.

Once again, the outsider shows the way. Like Naaman the Syrian, the Samaritan recognizes God's gift and returns to give thanks.

The word Eucharist means thanksgiving. Every Mass is our return to Jesus to thank him. Paul, writing from prison, shows that gratitude can survive even in suffering. "Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead," he says, and he adds, "But God's word isn't chained."

This week, be the one who comes back. Each evening, name three things you are grateful for and thank God for them. And thank someone who has helped you.
